title: grep & regular expressions
about: Searching text with grep: its options and exit status, basic and extended regular expressions, anchors, brackets, repetition, groups, and how regular expressions differ from shell wildcards.

questions.title: What grep does
questions.text: What does `grep pattern file` print?

options.t: Every line of `file` that contains text matching `pattern`.
options.why: It selects whole lines; it does not print only the matching word unless you ask with `-o`.

options.t: The names of the files that contain the pattern, without the lines themselves.
options.why: That is `grep -l`, or `grep -r` with a directory.

options.t: Only the first match in the whole file, and then it stops reading.
options.why: All matching lines are printed (unless `-m` limits them).

options.t: The number of matches, instead of the lines that contain the pattern.

questions.title: Where the text comes from
questions.text: What does `grep root` do with no file operand?

options.t: It reads standard input, so it can be used in the middle of a pipeline.
It searches the whole file system for files that contain the word, starting from `/`.
It fails with the error "missing file", because no file to search was given.
options.why: Like most filters it falls back to standard input.

options.t: It searches all the files of the current directory, without descending into directories.

questions.title: Common grep options
questions.text: Match each option with its effect.

pairs.r: Ignore case
Invert: print the lines that do NOT match
pairs.why: A way to filter things out.

pairs.r: Print the number of matching lines
Prefix each line with its line number
pairs.why: Helpful to find the place in an editor.

pairs.r: Print only the names of files with a match

questions.title: More grep options
questions.text: Match each option with its effect.

pairs.r: Search directories recursively
Print only the matched part of each line
pairs.why: Each match on its own line.

pairs.r: Match whole words only
The whole line must match
Treat the pattern as a fixed string, not as a regular expression
pairs.why: Dots and stars lose their meaning.

extras.r: Replace the match with another text

questions.title: Options that change what is printed
questions.text: Select the options that make `grep` print something other than the matching lines.

options.why: Only changes how the matching is done.

questions.title: Exit status of grep
questions.text: What exit status does `grep` return when it finds no match in a readable file?

options.why: 0 means at least one match, 1 no match, 2 an error (for example a missing file).

questions.title: grep statuses
questions.text: Match each command with its exit status.

pairs.why: Error: the file could not be read.

extras.why: Not produced by any of these.

questions.title: Quiet mode
questions.text: What does `grep -q root /etc/passwd` do, and why is it useful in `if`?

options.t: It prints nothing and only sets the exit status, so `if grep -q ...; then` can test for a pattern.
options.why: `-q` stops at the first match, too.

options.t: It prints the matching line without the colours that `grep` normally adds to it.
It quotes the pattern for the shell, so that special characters in it are kept safe.
options.why: Quoting is done by the shell.

options.t: It searches faster because it ignores the case of the letters in the file and in the pattern, which skips some comparisons.

questions.title: Case and count
questions.text: Which command counts how many lines contain `error` in any capitalisation?

options.why: Combined options: ignore case and count.
Prints lines with numbers, not a count.
Prints the lines without the word.

questions.title: Filtering out noise
questions.text: Which command shows the lines of `config` that are not comments (comments start with `#`)?

options.why: `-v` inverts; `^#` matches lines starting with a hash.

questions.title: Searching a tree
questions.text: Which command lists the files below `/etc` that contain the text `ssh`, printing only the file names?

options.why: Without `-r`, grep complains that `/etc` is a directory.
Also a directory error, and it would print counts.

questions.title: grep on file names versus contents
questions.text: What is the difference between `ls | grep foo` and `grep foo *`?

options.t: The first keeps the file names that contain `foo`; the second searches the text inside every file of the directory.
They do the same thing, because `grep` always looks at the names of the files.
The first searches inside the files of the directory, while the second looks only at the names of the files in it.
The second works only when the argument is a directory and fails for ordinary files.
options.why: It works on the files matching the glob `*`.

questions.title: Several files
questions.text: When `grep root /etc/passwd /etc/group` searches two files, how does the output change compared to one file?

options.t: Each line is prefixed with the name of the file it came from.
The output is sorted alphabetically, with the lines of both files mixed together.
Only the first file is searched, and the second one is ignored by `grep`.
Identical lines found in both files are merged into a single line of output.

questions.title: Context lines
questions.text: What does `grep -C 2 error log` add to the output?

options.t: Two lines of context before and after each matching line.
Two more matching lines after the first match, and then the search stops.
A count of two matches, printed at the end of the output of `grep`.
The last two lines of the file `log`, in addition to the matching lines.

questions.title: Context options
questions.text: Match each option with its effect.

pairs.r: Also print 3 lines after each match
Also print 3 lines before each match
3 lines before and after
Stop after 3 matching lines

questions.title: Pattern versus wildcard
questions.text: What is the most important difference between a regular expression and a shell wildcard (glob)?

options.t: A glob matches *file names* and is expanded by the shell; a regular expression matches *text* and is used by programs like `grep`.
options.why: Their symbols also mean different things.

options.t: There is no difference: both use the same symbols with the same meaning everywhere.
options.why: `*` means "anything" in a glob but "repeat the previous item" in a regex.

options.t: Regular expressions only work inside scripts, while globs work at the prompt.
options.why: They work on the command line.

options.t: Globs are more powerful than regular expressions, because the shell is a full language and expands them before any other program runs.
options.why: Regular expressions are far more expressive.

questions.title: Star in glob and regex
questions.text: Match each pattern with what it matches.

pairs.r: Any file name ending in `.txt`
Zero or more letters `a`
Any text, including nothing
pairs.why: A dot followed by a star: any character, repeated.

pairs.r: Exactly one character of a file name
Exactly one character of any kind
pairs.why: The regex counterpart of the glob `?`.

questions.title: Dot
questions.text: In a regular expression, what does `.` match?

options.why: Use `\.` to match a literal dot.

questions.title: Literal dot
questions.text: To match the text `c.t` but **not** `cat`, escape the dot: `grep 'c{{0}}t' file`
questions.note: Inside a bracket expression most special characters lose their meaning, so `[.]` is an equally good spelling.

wrong.why: Unescaped, the dot matches any character, so `cat` would match too.

questions.title: Anchors
questions.text: What do `^` and `$` match in a regular expression?

options.t: The start and the end of a line.
options.why: They do not match characters, but positions.

options.t: A literal caret and a literal dollar.
The start and end of a word.
The start and end of the file.

questions.title: Anchored patterns
questions.text: Match each pattern with the lines it selects.

pairs.r: Lines that start with `root`
Lines that end with `bash`
Empty lines
Lines that consist of exactly `root`

extras.why: `^` would need an escape or a bracket: `[\^]`.

questions.title: Counting empty lines
questions.text: Which command counts the empty lines of a file?

options.why: Start of line directly followed by end of line.
Every line has an end, so this counts all lines.
Counts lines that contain a space.

questions.title: Which lines does `^[A-Z]` select
questions.text: The pattern `^[A-Z]` requires the line to start with an upper-case letter. Classify each line.

items.why: A leading space: the first character is not a capital.

questions.title: Bracket expression
questions.text: What does the pattern `b[ae]g` match?

options.why: Exactly one character out of the set inside the brackets.
A bracket matches a single character.
One character from the set is required.

questions.title: Brackets in practice
questions.text: Match each pattern with what it matches.

pairs.r: One vowel
One digit
One character that is not a digit
pairs.why: The caret inside the bracket negates.

pairs.r: One ASCII letter
One blank, tab or other white-space character

extras.why: A bracket matches a single character; repeat it with `*` or `+` for a word.

questions.title: Caret meaning
questions.text: What are the two different meanings of the caret `^` in a regular expression?

options.t: Outside brackets it anchors the start of a line; as the first character inside brackets it negates the set.
It always negates the pattern that follows it, both inside and outside of brackets.
It always means the start of the line, also when it is the first character in a bracket, where it marks the start as well.
It means "or" between two alternatives, like the vertical bar does in `-E` patterns.

questions.title: Star and zero
questions.text: Given the lines `ac`, `abc`, `abbc`, `abbbc`, how many of them does `ab*c` match?

options.why: `b*` means zero or more `b`, so even `ac` matches.
The line `ac` has zero `b`, which `*` allows.
`*` would need to be exact for that.

questions.title: A star that matches everything
questions.text: Why does `grep 'f*' file` print every line of the file?

options.t: `f*` means zero or more `f`, and "zero `f`" matches at any position of any line.
options.why: A regex that can match the empty string matches all lines.

options.t: Because `*` is a wildcard that stands for all the files of the current directory.
options.why: That is a glob, not a regex.

options.t: Because `grep` ignores the patterns that contain a star and prints everything instead.
Because the file happens to contain only lines that have the letter `f` in them.

questions.title: Pattern for words
questions.text: Which pattern matches a line consisting of a four-letter word that starts with `c` and ends with `h` (such as `cash`)?

options.why: Matches inside longer words too, such as `catch`.
Only one character in the middle.

questions.title: Whole words
questions.text: Why is `grep -w cat` different from `grep cat`?

options.t: `-w` accepts `cat` only as a whole word, so `concatenate` and `cats` are not matched.
options.why: Word characters on either side block the match.

options.t: `-w` matches words written in any language, not only the English ones.
`-w` writes the matching words to a file instead of printing them on the screen.
`-w` makes the match case-insensitive, so `Cat` and `CAT` are found too.

questions.title: Three-letter b_g words
questions.text: A word of exactly three letters, starting with `b`, ending in `g`, with `a` or `e` in the middle: `grep -w 'b{{0}}g' words`
questions.note: A bracket expression works everywhere; alternation `a|e` needs extended syntax.

wrong.why: Alternation with parentheses needs `-E` (or a backslash) in basic expressions.

questions.title: Negated bracket
questions.text: Which words of `bag`, `beg`, `big`, `bog` does `b[^ae]g` match?

options.why: The middle character must be something other than `a` or `e`.
The set excludes two of them.

questions.title: -E
questions.text: What does the `-E` option (or the command `egrep`) change?

options.t: It enables extended regular expressions, where `+`, `?`, `|`, `{}` and `()` are operators without backslashes.
options.why: Easier to read than the basic dialect.

options.t: It makes the search case-insensitive, so that capital letters match lower case ones.
It prints only the part of each line that matches, instead of printing the whole line, one match per output line.
It excludes the lines that match, printing only those that do not contain the pattern.

questions.title: Repetition operators
questions.text: Match each operator with its meaning in extended regular expressions.

pairs.r: One or more of the previous item
Zero or one of the previous item
Zero or more of the previous item
Between two and four of the previous item
Exactly three of the previous item

extras.r: One or more of any character

questions.title: Basic versus extended plus
questions.text: In basic regular expressions (plain `grep`), what does `a+b` match?

options.t: The literal text `a+b`: `+` has no special meaning unless escaped (`a\+b`) or `-E` is used.
One or more letters `a` followed by the letter `b`, as in `aab` and `ab`.
Nothing: it is an invalid pattern that makes `grep` print an error message.
Any text at all, since the plus sign stands for any characters in a pattern, so every line of the file is printed.

questions.title: Optional letter
questions.text: Given the lines `ac`, `abc`, `abbc`, which does `grep -E 'ab?c'` select?

questions.title: Plain grep and question mark
questions.text: Given the same lines `ac`, `abc`, `abbc`, what does `grep 'ab?c'` (basic syntax, no `-E`) print?

options.t: Nothing, because in basic syntax `?` is an ordinary character and no line contains `ab?c`.
`ac` and `abc`, because `?` makes the preceding letter optional in every dialect of regular expressions, basic ones included.
All three lines, because `?` matches any single character in the middle.
An error about an invalid pattern, because a question mark needs `-E`.
options.why: The pattern is valid, just literal.

questions.title: Alternatives
questions.text: Print the lines that contain `cat` or `cut`: `grep -E 'cat{{0}}cut' file`
questions.note: In basic syntax the same is written `cat\|cut` with GNU grep.

wrong.why: There is no comma operator in regular expressions.
The shell uses that between commands; in a regex a single bar separates alternatives.

questions.title: Grouping alternatives
questions.text: Which pattern matches a line that consists of exactly `one` or exactly `two`?

options.why: The parentheses keep the anchors outside the alternation.
The anchors bind to the individual alternatives: lines starting with `one` or ending with `two`.
A bracket matches a single character.

questions.title: Anchors and alternation
questions.text: Why does `grep -E '^root|daemon'` match the line `the daemon runs`?

options.t: `^root` applies only to the first alternative; the second, `daemon`, matches anywhere on the line.
`-E` ignores the `^` anchor, so the pattern matches at any position in the line.
options.why: The anchor is honoured, but only for its own alternative.

options.t: Because `|` is a literal character in this pattern, so `daemon` is just part of a longer word that the line has to contain.
options.why: In `-E` it is the alternation operator.

options.t: Because the line happens to end with the word `daemon`, which the anchor selects.

questions.title: Repeated group
questions.text: What does `echo abcabc | grep -oE '(abc){2}'` print?

options.why: The input has only two copies.

questions.title: Backreference
questions.text: What does `\1` mean in `grep -E '(.)\1'`?

options.t: A repeat of whatever the first group matched, so the pattern finds two identical characters in a row.
The first character of the line, which the group `(.)` matches and then remembers for the rest of the pattern.
A literal digit `1`, which has to follow any character for the line to match.
options.why: After a backslash a digit refers to a group.

options.t: The first file given to `grep`, from which the matches are then printed.

questions.title: IP address shape
questions.text: Match something shaped like an IPv4 address (four groups of digits separated by dots): `grep -oE '[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+){{0}}'`
questions.note: Such a pattern accepts numbers like 999.1.1.1, so a validating script should also check the ranges.

wrong.why: The first group of digits is already written; with four repeats the address would have five parts.
That would accept any number of dotted groups, including none.

questions.title: Extended or basic
questions.text: Which of these commands behave the same?

options.why: GNU grep supports `\+` in basic mode.
The second looks for a literal plus.
In basic syntax `|` is a literal character.
The second looks for literal parentheses.

questions.title: Literal search
questions.text: You want to find lines containing the text `1.2.3` exactly, dots included. Which command is best?

options.why: Dots match any character, so `1x2y3` would match.

questions.title: Quoting patterns
questions.text: Why should a pattern such as `a*b` be put in quotes on the command line?

options.t: So that the shell does not treat `*` as a file-name wildcard before `grep` sees it.
options.why: Without quotes `a*b` may expand to existing file names.

options.t: Because `grep` refuses patterns without quotes and prints a syntax error instead.
options.why: It is the shell's expansion that causes trouble.

options.t: Because quotes are what turns the text into a regular expression for `grep`.
options.why: Patterns are regular expressions by default.

options.t: Because quotes make the search case-insensitive, like the option `-i` does.

questions.title: Searching for a dollar
questions.text: How do you search for the literal text `$HOME` in a file?

options.why: Single quotes keep the shell from expanding it; `-F` keeps `$` from being an anchor.
Double quotes let the shell replace it with your home path.
That looks for lines that start with `HOME`.

questions.title: Escaping a bracket
questions.text: Which pattern matches the literal text `[ERROR]` (with the square brackets)?

options.why: The backslashes make the brackets literal.
That matches any one of the letters E, R or O.

questions.title: Tab character
questions.text: A field in a file is separated by a tab. Which command reliably finds lines with a tab?

options.why: In basic syntax `\t` matches the letter `t`.
Matches every line with the letter `t`.

questions.title: Users without a login shell
questions.text: Which command prints the lines of `/etc/passwd` whose shell is `/usr/sbin/nologin`?

options.why: The shell is the last field; anchoring to the end is precise.
Lines do not start with it.

questions.title: Users with uid over 999
questions.text: Which pattern selects the lines of `/etc/passwd` where the third field is a number of four or more digits?

options.why: Two fields without colons, then four or more digits, then a colon.

options.t: `grep '[0-9]{4}' /etc/passwd`, with the braces taken literally in basic mode
options.why: Without `-E` the braces are literal; and it would match digits anywhere.

options.t: `grep -E '^[0-9]{4,}' /etc/passwd`, which looks at the start of the whole line
options.why: That looks at the start of the line, where the user name is.

options.t: `grep -w 1000 /etc/passwd`, which only finds the one specific number 1000

questions.title: Failed logins
questions.text: Which pipeline counts the failed SSH password attempts in an `auth.log` whose lines contain `Failed password`?

options.why: Counts the lines that do *not* match.
Counts the words of the entire log.

questions.title: Extract the IPs
questions.text: Which command prints only the IPv4 addresses found in `auth.log`, one per match?

options.why: Takes the first field of each line, not necessarily an address.

questions.title: Top attackers
questions.text: Put the stages in order to list the five IP addresses with the most failed logins in `auth.log`, most frequent first.

items.why: Extract the address from each line.
Group equal addresses and count them.
Rank by count and keep the top five.

questions.title: Which regex
questions.text: You must match the lines that contain the word `error` followed by one or more digits, such as `error42`. Which pattern does it?

options.why: A bracket for one digit, repeated at least once.
`*` allows zero digits, so `error` alone matches too.
Needs `-E` and accepts anything after `error`, not only digits.
Matches lines that have either part.

questions.title: grep and the shell
questions.text: After `grep -r "TODO" .`, you see many lines from files named `*.bak`. How can you skip those files?

options.why: GNU grep can exclude file names that match a glob.

options.t: `grep -r TODO . -v .bak`, where `-v` excludes the file names that match
`grep -r TODO .bak`, which searches the directory called `.bak` only
options.why: That searches a file or directory called `.bak`.

options.t: `grep -r -i TODO .`, which ignores the case of the letters in the files
